newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution rests in paratrooper race-murder case.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution rests in paratrooper race-murder case.

text.p: Prosecutors in the trial of an ex-private in the U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division accused of murdering a black couple, rested their case on Friday after showing pictures of a leather jacket with racist symbols they said was the defendant's.

Former paratrooper James Burmeister, who has been linked to a white supremacist skinhead group, is charged with first-degree murder of Jackie Burden and Michael James, shot and killed as they walked through a Fayetteville neighbourhood on Dec. 7, 1995.

Pictures showed the black leather jacket had a swastika sewn onto it and a reversed American flag with yellow border. Prosecutors said it was found in the car Burmeister and two other former soldiers from nearby Army base Fort Bragg, North Carolina were in the night of the killings.
A defence motion to dismiss the charges on grounds of insufficient evidence were denied by North Carolina Superior Court Judge Coy Brewer.

Prosecutors plan to seek the death penalty if a first-degree murder conviction is returned. They portrayed Burmeister, 21, from Thompson, Pennsylvania, as "pure unmitigated evil," saying he murdered the couple because they were black.

Randy Meadows, who was accused of driving Burmeister and Malcolm Wright, another white ex-soldier, to the area where the killings occurred, confessed and became the state's key witness against Burmeister.

Meadows was arrested minutes after the shooting when a police officer saw him sitting in the car. He told police he heard six gunshots after Burmeister and Wright got out of the car. He also said Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web" tattoo, a skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a homosexual or a black person.
Police found white supremacist literature, a Nazi flag and a book on how to make a bomb in Burmeister's trailer home.
The defence begins its case on Monday.
